The integration of antiretroviral therapy (ART) with tuberculosis (TB) treatment has been studied extensively, with evidence suggesting that early initiation of ART during TB treatment can reduce morbidity and mortality in individuals co-infected with HIV and TB. 2. The timing of ART initiation in HIV-1 infected individuals with TB has been a critical area of research, with studies indicating that earlier ART initiation, particularly in those with low CD4 counts, improves outcomes but may increase the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). 3. Research comparing earlier versus later initiation of ART in HIV-infected adults with TB has demonstrated that earlier ART initiation reduces overall mortality, though it requires careful management of potential complications such as IRIS. 4. Sub-analyses of clinical trials, such as the RAFA trial, are ongoing to further refine the understanding of ART and TB treatment integration. 5. Dolutegravir-based ART regimens have been evaluated in patients co-infected with TB and HIV, showing promising results in terms of efficacy and safety in multicenter, non-comparative, open-label, randomized trials. 6. Comparative studies of dolutegravir and efavirenz-based ART regimens for first-line HIV treatment have highlighted the superior efficacy and tolerability of dolutegravir, supporting its use in clinical practice. 7. Enhanced prophylaxis combined with ART has been shown to improve outcomes in individuals with advanced HIV infection in Africa, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive care strategies. 8. Guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and rapid ART initiation stress the need for thorough clinical assessment, including screening for TB and meningitis, before starting ART. 9. Early, time-limited ART in South African infants infected with HIV has been shown to significantly improve survival and reduce disease progression, as demonstrated in the CHER randomized trial. 10. Universal ART for HIV-infected children has been reviewed, with evidence supporting its benefits while also highlighting potential risks that must be managed during implementation. 11. Paradoxical TB-associated IRIS in children has been documented, with studies emphasizing the need for careful monitoring and management of this condition during ART initiation. 12. Prospective studies on IRIS in HIV-infected children from high-prevalence countries have provided valuable insights into its incidence, risk factors, and management strategies. 13. Observations from clinical settings, such as the Martin-Preuss Center in Malawi, suggest that initiating ART and TB treatment simultaneously is feasible and can be beneficial, though it requires careful clinical judgment. 14. Feasibility studies on ART initiation under the treat-all policy in routine conditions, such as in Eswatini, have demonstrated the practicality of this approach in real-world settings. 15. WHO guidelines on HIV disclosure counseling for children and adolescents emphasize the importance of age-appropriate communication and support for young individuals living with HIV. 16. Prednisone has been studied for the prevention of paradoxical TB-associated IRIS, with evidence supporting its use in specific clinical scenarios to mitigate inflammatory complications. 17. The impact of HIV-associated TB, TB-IRIS, and prednisone on lung function has been explored, highlighting the long-term respiratory consequences of these conditions. 18. Updated clinical considerations for rapid ART initiation recommend initiating ART while investigating for TB, with close follow-up to ensure timely TB treatment if diagnosed. 19. Rapid ART initiation has been recommended by WHO since 2017, with strong evidence supporting its benefits in reducing morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV. 20. Systematic screening for TB symptoms, as defined by WHO's four-symptom screening criteria, is essential before initiating same-day ART to minimize the risk of missed TB diagnoses. 21. Studies in Kenya and South Africa have shown that a significant proportion of individuals presenting for ART initiation are not eligible for same-day ART due to active TB or TB symptoms requiring further investigation. 22. The sensitivity and specificity of WHO's four-symptom TB screening approach vary, particularly among individuals already on ART, necessitating further refinement of screening strategies. 23. Same-day ART initiation has been shown to be feasible and acceptable in clinical trials, with high levels of patient satisfaction and successful implementation in various settings. 24. Clinical guidelines emphasize the importance of excluding meningitis and screening for cryptococcal infection in individuals with advanced HIV disease before initiating ART. 25. Close follow-up is critical to ensure that TB diagnostic results are acted upon promptly and that adverse events, including IRIS, are recognized and managed effectively. 26. HIV programs must provide adequate training for healthcare personnel to recognize TB symptoms, assess advanced HIV disease, and manage co-infections and complications. 27. Rapid diagnostic tests for TB and systems for timely return of results are essential to support the implementation of rapid ART initiation policies. 28. Patient education and support are necessary to promote early recognition of IRIS, manage adverse events, and ensure adherence to ART regimens.
